abstract: Single-particle cryoEM is increasingly applied to compositionally complex, coarsely purified samples, whose micrographs often contain contaminants, including crystalline ice, aggregates, grid support material, and residual ethane. This contamination is spatially localized, occupying only part of an otherwise usable image such that rejecting whole micrographs would discard usable particles along with the contaminant. As data collection and processing grow more automated with less manual curation, this contamination becomes a greater liability, with contaminant-associated picks entering the particle stack and negatively impacting 3D refinement. These observations have motivated the development of tools to exclude contaminated regions of the image from analysis. Here we present cryoFILTER (Fourier-Informed Learning with Transformers for Excluding contaminated Regions), a framework for spatially selective micrograph curation that combines information from real-space images with local Fourier-space features and broader spatial context. Across held-out datasets, we find that these representations are highly complementary, distinguishing contamination from particle-bearing ice more accurately than isolated real-space or Fourier-space representations alone. Applying cryoFILTER to representative datasets removes contaminant-associated picks that classification does not reliably reject, while preserving nearby usable particles. This filtering yields more isotropic and interpretable reconstructions, more reproducible 2D classification, and, in an E. coli lysate, improved recovery of distinct ribosomal states. We additionally developed a lightweight classifier that assigns each detected contaminant region to its likely physical source, which we envision will aid in assessing the relative merits of different grid preparation and data collection approaches. Given its speed and interpretability, we anticipate that cryoFILTER will help establish localized curation as an upstream component of cryoEM structure determination, connecting specimen quality, particle selection, and data acquisition.
